criterion_notes.c1: Examines household access to piped drinking water on premises from the general network in rural areas of Brazilian municipalities.
criterion_notes.c2: Plain wording: Clearly YES (include), as the study evaluates institutional and governance arrangements for rural drinking water supply—comparing systems implemented, owned/managed, and maintained by community water user associations (often under municipal concession contracts) versus local municipal governments/public utilities, alongside regional state-owned utilities (CESBs), participatory municipal mechanisms, and local electoral/media accountability. Narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: YES (include, though near the boundary with participatory project delivery). Unlike evaluations of generic NGO/donor hardware construction where the control group receives no infrastructure, both treatment (583 municipalities) and control (592 municipalities) groups implemented new rural small-scale piped water systems during 2000-2008; the treatment contrast isolates the legal/institutional ownership and operating structure of the service provider recorded in the National Basic Sanitation Survey (water user association vs. municipal government/public firm, plus regional CESB vs. local municipal main utility ownership), directly matching 'utility ownership or regulatory structure directly governing service access'. Qualitative interviews also document concrete institutional rules (concession contracts transferring supply responsibility, CESB corporate bylaws restricting rural investment, conditional mainline connection rules, and municipal bureaucratic requirements).
criterion_notes.c3: Contains primary and secondary empirical evidence: a municipal-level panel difference-in-differences analysis combined with multinomial probit kernel matching (2000-2010 Census, 2000-2008 PNSB, and Ipeadata across 1,008 matched project municipalities and 5,389 total municipalities), informed by 36 semi-structured telephone interviews with municipal officials, association presidents, regional utility staff, and sector experts.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports municipal rural (and urban/total) access rates to piped drinking water on premises from the general network in 2000 and 2010 and the 2000-2010 change in connection rates.
criterion_notes.c5: Population and unit of analysis (Brazilian municipalities, measuring rural population access rates; N=5,389 municipalities in full DiD, N=1,008 municipalities / 1,899 municipality-year observations in kernel-matched DiD comparing 583 user-association and 592 local-government project municipalities; plus 36 key-informant interviews), exposure (provider ownership/governance type in rural districts and accountability/main-utility variables), outcome (change in rural piped-water connection rate on premises), and study design (quasi-experimental DiD with propensity-score kernel matching + qualitative interviews) are all clearly specified.
criterion_notes.c6: Full text is written in English.

evidence_quotes.quote: This paper investigates whether small-scale water supply systems implemented and operated by water user associations increase access to piped water supply in rural Brazil by more than systems by local governments.
In most cases, the local government only signs a concession contract to transfer responsibility for water supply to the association.

Such providers can be regional ﬁrms (CESB), local municipality governments or local (public) ﬁrms owned by the municipality, water user associations, private supply ﬁrms, and intermunicipal or interfederal cooperations.

As the eﬀect of project type on access rates might be confounded by simultaneous drivers of project-type choice and access rates, the quantitative analysis is based on a diﬀerence-in-diﬀerence estimator in combination with kernel matching to overcome the endogeneity of project type.
Table 1 shows access rates to piped water on premises from the general network in Brazil in the year 2000 and their increase from 2000 to the year 2010.

raw_response.exposure: Institutional/legal provider ownership and management form of new small-scale rural water supply systems implemented during 2000-2008 (community water user associations vs. local municipal governments/public utilities; also local vs. regional state-owned CESB main utility providers, municipal participatory mechanisms, and local political accountability channels)
raw_response.outcome: Rural (and urban/total) household access rate to piped drinking water on premises from the general network at the municipality level (2000-2010 change in connection share)
raw_response.population_and_sample: Rural populations of Brazilian municipalities (unit of analysis: municipality; full panel N = 5,389 municipalities / 10,448 observations in 2000 and 2010; kernel-matched comparison sample N = 1,008 municipalities / 1,899 observations drawn from 583 municipalities with new water user association systems and 592 municipalities with new local government systems; plus 36 semi-structured key-informant interviews)
raw_response.rationale: Barde (2017) empirically evaluates how the institutional ownership and management structure of rural piped-water service providers affects rural household connection rates across Brazilian municipalities between 2000 and 2010. Both treatment and control municipalities established new small-scale rural water supply systems during 2000-2008, isolating the provider/ownership regime (autonomous or concession-holding community water user associations vs. municipal governments/public firms, alongside regional state-owned utilities vs. municipal utilities) rather than merely comparing infrastructure presence vs. absence. Although framed partly in terms of participatory vs. non-participatory project choice and local electoral/media accountability, its core exposure directly examines utility/provider ownership and governance structure governing water service access, satisfying all inclusion criteria (c1-c6) under both the plain wording and the 2026-10-13 narrow reading of Criterion 2.
raw_response.study_design: Mixed-methods: quasi-experimental municipal panel difference-in-differences combined with multinomial probit propensity-score kernel matching, informed by 36 semi-structured interviews
